title: Research & Projects
text:
Astrophysics

Search for Quasi-Periodic Oscillations in Gamma-Ray Bursts

Sep. 2026 - Present | Supervisor: Prof. Ersin Göğüş (Sabancı University)

I analyze Fermi/GBM light curves across different time intervals and energy bands to search for candidate quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in gamma-ray bursts.

Modeling power spectra using power-law continua and Lorentzian profiles with Python and Stingray.
Using Gaussian Process modeling to characterize stochastic background variability and test whether candidate signals remain significant after accounting for analysis choices and multiple trials.
Checking the energy dependence of candidate features and comparing findings with published studies.

Fermi/GBM Stingray Gaussian Processes High-Energy Astrophysics


Quasi-Periodic Oscillation Analysis of V1405 Cas Using TESS Photometry

Oct. 2025 - Present | Supervisor: Prof. Ersin Göğüş (Sabancı University)

I study how oscillatory signals evolve in V1405 Cas (a classical nova and cataclysmic variable) as the system relaxes following an outburst.

Extended previous studies by identifying and adding two new post-outburst TESS sectors, increasing the time baseline for tracking variability.
Comparing pre-outburst and post-outburst power spectra sector by sector, fitting Gaussian and Lorentzian models to candidate QPO features.
Estimating detection significance and upper limits during phases where signals are weak, separating real accretion-driven variability from instrumental or pipeline artifacts.

TESS Photometry Cataclysmic Variables Power Spectral Analysis


Exoplanet Light Curve Formation and Calibration with TESS Photometry

Jan. 2024 - Present | Supervisor: Asst. Prof. Tansu Daylan (Washington University in St. Louis / @AstroMusers)

A long-term project focused on catalog-scale transit analysis of confirmed and candidate exoplanet targets observed by TESS.

Built reproducible Python pipelines to clean, detrend, normalize, and phase-fold TESS-SPOC and QLP light curves.
Applied Box Least Squares (BLS) periodograms to recover orbital periods, transit durations, and transit depths.
Systematically compared recovered parameters against ExoFOP-TESS and literature catalogs, diagnosing discrepancies caused by detrending artifacts, period aliases, or depth dilution.
Currently calculating expected timing precision limits from finite light-curve baselines as part of a manuscript in preparation.

Exoplanets TESS Box Least Squares Time-Series Pipelines

title: Research & Projects
section: Condensed Matter, Quantum Systems & Field Theory
text:
Condensed Matter, Quantum Systems & Field Theory

Connectivity Conditions for Nagaoka Ferromagnetism in Honeycomb Lattices (Senior Thesis)

Dec. 2025 - May 2026 | Supervisors: Prof. Alev Devrim Güçlü (İzmir Institute of Technology) & Asst. Prof. Emir Haliki (Ege University)

For my undergraduate thesis, I investigated when and how finite honeycomb lattice structures satisfy the connectivity requirements for Nagaoka ferromagnetism.

Built triangular and hexagonal honeycomb clusters with varying boundary conditions and zigzag/armchair edges.
Modeled the one-hole Hubbard limit by mapping hole motion and spin configurations onto a connected state graph.
Used breadth-first search (BFS) algorithms to test reachability across many-body states under nearest-neighbor hopping and analyze finite-size effects.

Senior Thesis Hubbard Model Graph Algorithms Computational Physics


Graphene Quantum Dots - Tight-Binding Modeling (Research Internship)

Aug. 2025 - Sep. 2025 | Supervisor: Prof. Alev Devrim Güçlü (İzmir Institute of Technology)

During my summer internship at IZTECH, I built tight-binding models from scratch to study the electronic properties of finite graphene structures.

Started from a six-site benzene-like ring and scaled up to hexagonal and triangular graphene quantum dots with zigzag and armchair edges.
Computed energy spectra, density of states (DOS), and site-resolved probability densities.
Extended the model to include next-nearest-neighbor hopping to study symmetry breaking, mid-gap states, and edge localization.

Tight-Binding Graphene Quantum Dots Electronic Structure


Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) & Casimir Effect in Curved Spacetime

Undergraduate Research (~1.5 Years) | Ege University

During my undergraduate studies, I spent roughly a year and a half working with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and exploring the Casimir effect in curved spacetime. This work also sparked my ongoing interest in Quantum Field Theory (QFT), particularly its mathematical foundations and geometric aspects.

title: Enes Yakut
text:
Hi! I am a physics graduate from Ege University (2026), preparing to start my M.S. studies in Physics. My primary work focuses on time-domain astrophysics and computational physics, particularly high-energy variability, astrophysical data analysis, and numerical modeling.
Over the past two years, I have worked on extracting and validating signals from noisy astronomical time-series data. With Dr. Tansu Daylan (Washington University in St. Louis), I analyze TESS light curves to refine exoplanet transit parameters across catalog-scale samples. In collaboration with Prof. Ersin Göğüş (Sabancı University), I study quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in accretion-driven systems like the classical nova V1405 Cas using TESS photometry, as well as searching for QPO signatures in gamma-ray bursts with Fermi/GBM data.
Alongside astrophysics, I completed my undergraduate thesis in computational condensed matter physics with Prof. Alev Devrim Güçlü (İzmir Institute of Technology) and Dr. Emir Haliki (Ege University), modeling Nagaoka ferromagnetism and graphene quantum dots from first principles. Earlier during my undergraduate studies, I also spent about a year and a half working with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to study the Casimir effect in curved spacetime, and I continue to have a strong interest in Quantum Field Theory (QFT), especially its mathematical foundations.




Time-Domain & High-Energy Astrophysics: Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs), gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), cataclysmic variables, and accretion-driven variability
Exoplanet Photometry: Transit light curve modeling, detrending pipelines, and catalog-scale parameter validation (TESS)
Quantum Field Theory & Mathematical Physics: Mathematical structure of QFT, quantum effects in curved spacetime, and the Casimir effect
Scientific Computing & Machine Learning in Physics: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), time-series analysis, power spectral modeling, Gaussian Processes, and numerical simulations

💬 Open to Discussion: Whether you have questions, want to exchange ideas, or just want to chat about any of the topics above - from TESS light curves and QPOs to tight-binding models, PINNs, or the mathematical side of QFT - feel free to reach out anytime at enessyakut@outlook.com.

title: Modeling Power Spectra in QPO Searches
text:
When searching for quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in X-ray or optical light curves, we rarely look for a strictly sinusoidal peak on top of white noise. Instead, accretion-driven systems and gamma-ray bursts typically show broadband stochastic variability (“red noise”) that must be modeled alongside any candidate signal.

Continuum + Lorentzian Model
A common approach is to model the power spectral density P(\nu) as a power-law continuum plus a Lorentzian profile for the candidate QPO feature:

P(\nu) = A \nu^{-\alpha} + C + \frac{R^2 \, \frac{\Delta}{\pi}}{\Delta^2 + (\nu - \nu_0)^2}

where:

A \nu^{-\alpha} captures the red-noise power-law continuum with slope \alpha,
C is the white-noise (Poisson) level at high frequencies,
\nu_0 is the centroid frequency of the candidate oscillation,
\Delta is the half-width at half-maximum (HWHM), related to the quality factor by Q = \frac{\nu_0}{2\Delta}.



Why Detrending and Continuum Choices Matter
In practice, whether a peak looks statistically significant depends strongly on how the underlying continuum is parameterized. Testing alternative background models - and accounting for the number of frequencies and time/energy intervals searched - is essential before claiming a physical oscillation.
